idiom_name: pure abstract class (pure virtual functions + public virtual destructor)
implementation_notes: The classic C++ realization: a class with only public pure virtual functions and a public virtual destructor, no data members, and deleted copy operations so instances cannot be sliced. C++ has no interface keyword, so the contract is a declaration and naming discipline - but the essential part is still compiler-enforced: a class whose final overrider is pure virtual cannot be instantiated. What replaces the interface keyword is therefore = 0 plus conventions (I-prefixed names, empty abstract classes as interfaces per Core Guidelines I.25/C.121). Keep this form when implementations are chosen at run time and clients hold pointers or references to the contract.
pitfalls: Forgetting the public virtual destructor makes deleting through the contract undefined behaviour; a pure virtual destructor must still be defined out of line, because destructors are always called along the chain.
Allowing copies of the contract invites slicing (a Square copied into a Shape value); delete the copy operations, or hide copying behind an explicit virtual clone().
Calling a pure virtual function from a constructor or destructor is undefined behaviour, so contract invariants cannot be enforced through the contract's constructor.

A polymorphic contract without an out-of-line key function makes every translation unit that deletes through it depend on the compiler's vtable placement, which hurts ABI stability across shared libraries.

variants.name: Concept-constrained interface (compile-time contract)
variants.implementation_notes: A C++20 concept names the requirements as a compile-time predicate and a template consumes it, so the contract is checked during overload resolution and the implementation is instantiated directly: no vtable, no virtual destructor, no boxing, and calls stay inlinable. This is the type-class-style realization - bounded, statically resolved polymorphism - and the one to choose when every implementor is known at compile time, when the contract is about what a type can do rather than about an object's identity, or when operators must be part of the contract (the Core Guidelines document template parameters with concepts, I.9). It does not replace the runtime contract where implementors arrive at run time or cross a binary boundary: concepts are erased after compilation and each instantiation is a distinct type.
pitfalls: A concept checks that expressions are well formed, not that they mean what the contract promises - semantics still need documentation and tests.
Every instantiation is a distinct type, so two implementors cannot share one container or one ABI boundary; use std::unique_ptr<Shape> there.
Concepts with many atomic requirements produce diagnostics that are hard to attribute, and changing the concept invalidates every template that named it.
